title: The Muscle-Powered Moonberries
markdown:
The moon hung in a sliver. Mila the inventor, in her cozy cottage with Pip the cinnamon-furred fox, had a problem that made the forest feel glum. Dr. Rowan’s prize moonpetal flowers were wilting.

“They need moonberry nectar,” he sighed. “But the berries are all the way up the Whispering Rock.”

The rock was tall, smooth, too slippery to climb. Pip’s ears drooped.

“How can we reach them? We must help the garden.” His tail thumped anyway, which is fox for we will try.

First attempts were a bit silly. Pip scrambled; claws found no grip. Slide. Down. “Too slippery!” Mila tried pine sap. Hands gooey, Pip sticky, berries still high. Pip shook sap from a whisker and did not call the feeling names.

Mila sat and watched. A spider anchored each thread with care. A robin landed — not a mere hop. Wings pushed. Legs bent at a useful point and pulled the body on.

“Pip. The robin doesn’t only push with its feet. It pulls with its whole body. Wing down, then the leg bends and hauls it up. Something inside works together.”

She tapped her upper arm. “When I bend at the elbow, this forearm comes closer. Same at the knee.” She bent it. “Muscles pull on bones, right at the joints. The bone comes closer. That is how I move.”

Pip’s ears twitched. “So the robin uses muscles to pull itself, even on slippy stuff?”

“Exactly. Strong bands. Climbing, we grip, then pull, bending at elbows, knees, shoulders.”

They went back to the Whispering Rock. “Leg muscles pull the lower leg when you bend the knee,” Mila said. “Do that as you push off with the other foot. Then arm muscles, pull.”

Pip set a paw, then another. Bent his knees, a small push, pulled with his arms, elbows folding. Slowly, up. Mila found nubs for fingers. A new rhythm: pull, bend, pull. Slow. Steady. No sap required.

The top. Moonberries gleamed, plump, ready. A basketful. Pride, which weighs less than sap. Descent careful. The forest floor did not need to sigh; the flowers would.

At Dr. Rowan’s, nectar on the wilting petals. They unfurled, silvery sheen returning, sweet air filling the cottage.

“Mila, Pip, you are simply wonderful. You saved my moonpetals.”

Pip nudged Mila, tail wagging, looking at a paw. “All that pulling and bending.”

Mila named it without a flourish. “Muscles pull bones at joints. Joints work like tiny hinges. Push, pull, through the world. Birds, spiders, us on that rock.”

Pip wiggled his toes, repeating it so it would stick. The moon had grown a little brighter, which moons do without being asked. They walked home with empty basket and working hinges, and Pip, still faintly pine-scented, practised a knee-bend on the path just to feel the pull.
